vorschau.en: My personal history of generating designs started in 2002 with a project that was called “Design Generator”. It was a physically based system implemented with a physics engine of 3D Studio …

inhalt:
Meine persönliche Geschichte des Generierens von Entwürfen begann 2002 mit einem Projekt namens „Entwurfsgenerator“. Es war ein physikbasiertes System, umgesetzt mit einer Physik-Engine von 3D Studio Max. Die Beziehungen zwischen räumlichen Einheiten wurden als Federn dargestellt, die Räume selbst als physikalische Körper. Die Verteilung der farbig markierten Funktionen wird durch anziehende und abstoßende Kräfte zwischen ihnen gesteuert.
Dieses erste Experiment ergab schöne Animationen, wie das Video unten zeigt. Das Modell wurde für den Entwurf eines Areals für Medienkünstler und Unternehmer in München umgesetzt.

Video auf Vimeo ansehen ↗

Eine ausführlichere Dokumentation auf Deutsch gibt es auf dieser älteren Website. Der Prozess ist in dieser Broschüre dokumentiert:

entwurfsgenerator.inhalt:
a parametric design

"...neither a thing nor a concept, but a continual flux or process"
William Morton Wheeler

Using the example of the Medien-Werk-Stadt, a center for new media that the City of Munich had planned for the former Beutler site at the corner of Ganghoferstraße and Ridlerstraße, a computer-generated design process was developed. The aim was to support the architect in designing by using the computing machine. The architect was to be freed from constraining mathematical tasks in order to expand his creative scope. In this context, the design process is dominated above all by functional considerations. A machine can solve these far faster and with far greater complexity than humans can.

prozess-1.inhalt:
first step
primary relations

Using values from 0 to 100, the primary relations define how strongly the individual building parts of the space allocation program are related to one another. High values mean that the parts will move closer to each other; low values result in a more neutral relationship. The effect of these relations can be imagined as that of a spring or rubber band, which is the stronger, the higher the defined value. The entire system strives for a stable equilibrium in which the sum of the spring tensions reaches its lowest value. If one value is changed, the entire structure is set in motion until it settles into a new equilibrium.

For example, the congress–lecture relation has a high value of 80, which will lead to spatial proximity. Congress–museum is defined as 20; here spatial proximity is considered less important.

prozess-2.inhalt:
second step
secondary relations

The secondary relations define the behavior of the rooms within the building parts. Individual rooms, such as ancillary rooms, are assigned the behavior of merging with the ancillary rooms within other higher-level parts as soon as they approach one another, but of abandoning this behavior again beyond a certain distance. These relational fields are comparable to magnetic fields, by which the areas strongly attract each other as soon as they come close. The magnitude of the value indicates the spatial extent of this field. The system of these dependencies is illustrated on the opposite page.

For example, the foyer areas have high values and thus a large surrounding force field. A merging of these areas is therefore strongly favored. Cleaning and sanitary storage rooms have low values; merging them was considered less important.

prozess-3.inhalt:
third step
open space affinity

The open space affinity value indicates how intensely open spaces attach themselves to the individual parts of the space allocation program. Open spaces are implemented as invisible bodies that displace the building parts and thus create voids.

For example, the museum needs only little open space around it and therefore has the value 20. For the apartments, open spaces were considered important, which is why they have the value 85.

prozess-4.inhalt:
The shape stability values indicate the need for the building parts to occupy a small surface area relative to their extent. A high value means a rather rigid, spherical body; a low value a fluid body without a stable shape.

For example, the congress building must have a coherent volume in order to function. It therefore has a high value of 95. The internet café or the museum could be distributed linearly or in a network throughout the complex; they therefore have low values of 20–30.

prozess-5.inhalt:
fifth step
implementation

The system was implemented in 3D Studio MAX, an animation program with the capability of simulating physical systems. The scripting language integrated into the program was used.

The process described is about finding the state in which the sum of all occurring tensions is lowest. Experiments showed that the final state of the process depends on the initial position of the building parts. If the initial position of the building parts is changed, different final states result from the same values. However, this should not be interpreted as a flaw in the process; rather, it is a genuine many-body problem, as known from physics.
The illustrations below show the relationship in two dimensions, whereas in reality the problem is three-dimensional. As in physics, the unique state of lowest energy can be reached with high probability by introducing chaotic motion (temperature) and gradually reducing this motion (cooling). This was not done in our process because, as shown below, a functionally unambiguous correct solution cannot be determined in architecture. Moreover, aesthetic, urban design, cultural and other criteria have not yet been taken into account and will be incorporated later.

Particles ("atoms") are implemented and enclosed by a flexible envelope for each building part.
The particles are connected to each other by spring tensions (the magnitude of the tensions determines the shape stability of the building part)
All particles of a building part are connected to the particles of the other building parts by spring tensions (the magnitude of the tensions determines the primary relations)

Some particles of a building part are surrounded by a force field that reacts to the force fields of particles of the same type (the field radius determines the secondary relations)

prozess-6.inhalt:
sixth step
Gaussian normal distribution

The defined values are soft, i.e., chosen subjectively. The state of the system is discrete, i.e., small changes in value lead to very different results. The base values are therefore varied by means of a Gaussian normal distribution in order to objectify them. The values change predominantly within the range of +10 to -10.
Outlier values such as 0 or 100 are set only rarely, as the frequency distribution shows.

prozess-7.inhalt:
seventh step
evolutionary development strategy

Through the fluctuation of the values, the computer becomes a tool for generating diverse variations of functional relationships. Once the structures begin to repeat, the process is interrupted and broken down into individual snapshots. Now the work of the interdisciplinary design team begins: they examine and differentiate the variants according to the usual criteria such as urban context, functionality, aesthetic power, construction and economic efficiency. Variants that show little potential for a high-quality design are sorted out; for others that have weaknesses in certain areas, the data set is crossed with those that are strong there. Scattering (mutation), which again varies the parameters by means of the Gaussian normal distribution, often produces configurations with new, positive properties. In this way, over several runs, variants are deliberately bred that have maximally positive characteristics.


Fig. from: das schriftbild der neuen musik [Notation in New Music],
erhard karkoschka
Drawing: Cage: Cartridge Music. Sheet 7

In a conventional design process, the architect first has to spend days working through the space allocation program before arriving at a first design that draws on the knowledge and experience of the designer and discards options that seem nonsensical. The drawback of this approach can be seen precisely in the pragmatic, unconscious preselection by the designer, who may thereby miss important possible solutions. Because of the high complexity, one easily tends to keep elaborating the concept, which is usually based on initial priorities, instead of questioning it again and forming new variants. The Design Generator is fed with the space allocation program and functional relationships in a short time and immediately computes any number of variants that sensibly lay out the spatial zones. The designer, in this case the design team, can devote itself entirely to discussion and selection. The evolutionary program is not determined by the imprints and preconceived, supposedly factual opinions of an individual designer. This gives rise to creative solutions that a human designer could not have produced.

The evolutionary process amounts to a search in a space of possible variants. In mathematics, 'space' is generally understood as a set of elements, for example points, vectors, functions, etc., between which certain relations exist. Genetic crossover searches this space and combines different good properties, which leads to new regions of the space in which better variants can be found. Mutation, on the other hand, can find the best variants in the immediate neighborhood.

The site marks a difficult location in urban design terms. Continuing the existing building volumes creates new constraints; forming a joint likewise creates problems. The selected variant, by contrast, fits meaningfully into the surrounding urban fabric. It is convincing because of an open area in the northeast as a counterpart to an open area opposite and as an entrance area to the entire complex with a central internet café. The open area along the railway lines was also assessed positively. Future greening seemed sensible here. The museum and training wing marks the intersection of Ganghoferstraße with the railway lines and creates a counterweight to the buildings opposite. The interlocking of research and living areas should foster a productive working climate.
The selected variant can serve as the basis for an overall design, sensibly predetermine a spatial arrangement of zones, or merely serve as inspiration. One goal is further development that allows orthogonal structures to be generated.

ausstellung.inhalt:
Exhibition

In the summer of 2002, through the mediation of Prof. Dr. Ulrich Winko and Prof. Sigi Bucher, the communications agency Kochan & Partner from Munich approached us to realize a pavilion and an exhibition on the topic of “parametric design”. One of the largest advertising agencies in Munich was looking for a new corporate vision and considered it worthwhile to present the potential of the new design method to its employees and clients. The intention was to explore shared possibilities of new developments in architecture and in the fields of graphics and advertising.
The project was realized in close collaboration with Ulrich Winko and Sigi Bucher in the conceptual phase, as well as with the composer and sound artist Ulrich Müller. He developed an interactive sound installation that reacts to the movements of visitors in the space and thus controls the flow of information. This made it possible to create an intense connection between the newly created and the existing spaces and the communication of content and its sonic design. Owing to the visitors' positive response to the spatial effect of the pavilion, the company Kochan & Partner decided to keep it after the exhibition and to use it as a contemplative retreat for employees and as a stimulating meeting room. Following this successful outcome, all participants are continuing their collaboration in a loose association.

Fig. from: das schriftbild der neuen musik [Notation in New Music], erhard karkoschka
Score: Hashagen: Cymbalon. Opening

Outlook
The question of the new role of the architect can be taken up at this point. If one considers extending the defining parameters in the course of the design, insights that have emerged during the design process can be incorporated. In design, the architect combines art and science and attempts to formalize results from these fields and feed them into computer-aided design. He defines, so to speak, the intersection between the pragmatic needs given by the building process and the far-reaching relationships that he constructs abstractly from the context (environment). This is where the architect's individual influence is shifted: he is no longer an artist who invents forms, but a thinker who defines and translates influences: he no longer constructs load-bearing structures from steel, wood or concrete, but from the intellectual potential of his time.

Against this background, we are working on the further development of the concept of computer-aided design and are looking for parallel developments in other fields. One example hinted at in the illustration above would be to explore the possible influence of New Music on architectural design, in the hope of mutual enrichment. Modern composers have long used new media technologies for composition. An exemplary case of a connection of music, architecture and modern natural science is Iannis Xenakis, who achieved this in a visionary way in his designs and compositions. The Design Generator follows similar principles to the musical composition programs of Xenakis, which are likewise based on statistical probability fields.
